description: Why health promotion matters, who delivers it, and how it supports individuals to change.
hero_image_caption: Community health workers delivering a health promotion session at a local centre.
content_html:
What Is Health Promotion?

Health promotion covers the full range of activities — from a leaflet in a GP waiting room to a national television campaign — that are designed to improve the health and well-being of individuals and communities. In health and social care, understanding the role and purpose of health promotion is not just a theoretical exercise: practitioners at every level are involved in promoting health, whether they are a support worker encouraging a service user to walk more, a school nurse delivering a healthy eating session, or a community health champion running a stop-smoking group.

The Role and Purpose of Health Promotion

The specification identifies four overlapping purposes of health promotion. First, health promotion aims to raise awareness of health and well-being issues — many people do not know, for instance, that they may have high blood pressure, or that they are drinking more alcohol than is safe. Raising awareness through campaigns, screenings and information is the foundation of any health promotion effort.

Second, health promotion aims to increase individuals’ positive lifestyle choices. It is not enough to tell people that smoking is harmful; effective health promotion provides the information, motivation and practical support needed for someone to quit. The goal is to shift from knowledge to behaviour change — from knowing that exercise is good to actually doing it regularly.

Third, health promotion works to reduce risks to health and well-being. By encouraging vaccination, safer sexual practices, reduced alcohol consumption, and regular physical activity, health promotion addresses the major modifiable risk factors for the UK’s most common chronic conditions, including cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, and some cancers.

Fourth — and this is the angle that is specific to this qualification and often tested — health promotion aims to reduce health and social care costs. A person who develops type 2 diabetes because of a preventable lifestyle factor will require ongoing NHS treatment, medications, and potentially social care support in later life. Every person who makes a positive lifestyle change, or who is screened and treated early, reduces the demand on publicly funded services. Health promotion is therefore not only a moral priority but an economic one.

Key Fact

The four purposes of health promotion are: raise awareness of health issues; increase positive lifestyle choices; reduce risks to health and well-being; and reduce health and social care costs. The cost-reduction purpose is frequently tested — prevention is cheaper than treatment.

Supporting Individuals to Take Responsibility

One of the most significant shifts in modern health and social care has been the move towards supporting individuals to take responsibility for their own health and well-being, rather than treating them as passive recipients of services. This approach recognises that lasting behaviour change is more likely when the individual is an active participant in their own health journey — not when they are simply told what to do.

Supporting individuals to take responsibility involves three main strategies. The first is prevention and control — providing individuals with the information and tools they need to prevent health problems before they arise or to manage existing conditions effectively. A GP practice running a pre-diabetes prevention programme, or a district nurse teaching a diabetic patient how to monitor their own blood glucose, are both examples of this approach.

The second strategy is educating by providing information and advice. This includes face-to-face consultations with health professionals, written materials such as leaflets and health promotion booklets, online resources, and community health events. The purpose of education is to equip individuals with the knowledge they need to make positive lifestyle choices — but providing information alone is rarely enough. Individuals also need to feel that the changes are achievable and relevant to their own lives. A health professional who provides culturally appropriate information, in a person’s first language, and at the right literacy level, is more likely to enable behaviour change than one who hands over a generic leaflet.

The third strategy is encouraging individuals to utilise their own strengths and informal networks. Rather than creating dependency on services, effective health promotion builds on what individuals already have — their social relationships, community connections, personal capabilities, and previous experience of managing difficulties. A person who is supported to recognise that they have already successfully made one health change (for example, cutting out sugary drinks) is more likely to believe they can make another. Informal networks — family, friends, faith communities, and workplace colleagues — can also be powerful sources of support for behaviour change.

Key Fact

Three strategies for supporting individuals to take responsibility: prevention and control (information and tools to prevent or manage conditions); educating through information and advice (knowledge that enables positive choices); and encouraging use of personal strengths and informal networks (building on what the individual already has rather than creating service dependency).

The Role of Campaigns, Education and Strengths-Based Approaches

At a national level, health campaigns are a key vehicle for raising awareness and enabling choice at scale. Campaigns such as Change4Life (now part of the NHS Better Health platform) and Stoptober reach millions of people through television, social media, GP surgeries and schools. Their power lies in their reach — no individual practitioner can achieve population-level impact alone.

At an individual level, a strengths-based approach in care settings shifts the focus from what a person cannot do to what they already can. A care worker using a strengths-based approach might ask: “What has helped you manage your health in the past?” and “Who in your life could support you with this?” This approach is consistent with the principles of active participation and person-centred care covered earlier in this unit — it treats the service user as the expert on their own life.

Health promotion operates at both local and national levels. At a national level, campaigns are coordinated by Public Health England (now the UK Health Security Agency) and NHS England, using mass media, social media, and GP referral programmes. At a local level, councils, GP surgeries, schools, voluntary organisations, pharmacies and community groups all play a role. For example, a local authority might fund a walking group for older adults, a school might run a mental health awareness week, or a pharmacy might offer free blood pressure checks. The most effective health promotion connects national campaigns with local delivery, so that the message reaches individuals in their own communities through trusted local contacts.
exam_tip_html: Questions on promoting health and well-being often use the command word ‘Discuss’, which requires you to consider more than one angle — for example, both the benefits of health promotion (to individuals and to the health and social care system) and the challenges (individuals may not engage, campaigns may not reach all groups). Remember to include the ‘reduce health and social care costs’ purpose — this is frequently missed by students who focus only on the individual benefits. For 6-mark questions, aim to give two developed points from different perspectives, each using “because” or “therefore” to show the reasoning chain. A strong answer might contrast a national campaign approach with a strengths-based individual approach, noting what each does well and where each has limitations.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Health promotion has four purposes: raise awareness of health issues; increase positive lifestyle choices; reduce risks to health and well-being; and reduce health and social care costs. The fourth purpose is the most frequently tested in exam questions.
  • Supporting individuals to take responsibility involves three strategies: prevention and control; education through information and advice; and encouraging individuals to use their own strengths and informal networks rather than becoming dependent on services.
  • Effective health promotion combines national campaigns (which achieve population-level reach) with local delivery (which reaches individuals through trusted local contacts and person-centred approaches).

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is one of the four purposes of promoting health and well-being?
A) Diagnosing conditions at an early stage
B) Reducing health and social care costs
C) Providing individual treatment plans
D) Increasing access to prescription medication
practice_questions.marks: B) Reducing health and social care costs [1 mark]. Diagnosis, treatment plans and prescription access are clinical activities rather than health promotion purposes.

practice_questions.text: Give two reasons why health promotion is important for the NHS and social care sector.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for two distinct reasons (max 2). Acceptable answers: health promotion reduces demand on NHS services by preventing conditions before they develop [1]; health promotion reduces the long-term costs of treating preventable chronic conditions such as type 2 diabetes [1]; raising awareness means conditions are identified and treated earlier, reducing severity and therefore the level of care needed [1]; enabling positive lifestyle choices reduces the number of people who develop conditions linked to modifiable risk factors [1]. Two near-identical points score 1 mark only.

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by a 'strengths-based approach' to supporting individuals to improve their health.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for the core meaning (identifying and building on the individual's existing strengths, capabilities and resources rather than focusing on deficits); 1 mark for a developed reason using 'because' (e.g. because individuals are more likely to sustain behaviour change when they feel capable and are using resources they already have); 1 mark for a specific practical example (e.g. a health worker asks a service user what has helped them manage their health successfully in the past and encourages them to use those same strategies rather than relying solely on professional support).

practice_questions.text: Describe how a GP surgery could use two different strategies to support patients to take responsibility for their own health and well-being.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks per strategy, applied to the GP surgery context. Education through information and advice (2 marks): 1 mark for naming the strategy; 1 mark for a specific GP surgery example (e.g. the practice provides patients with written information and a referral to an online health programme about managing pre-diabetes, giving them the knowledge and tools to make dietary and exercise changes). Encouraging use of personal strengths and informal networks (2 marks): 1 mark for naming the strategy; 1 mark for a specific example (e.g. the GP asks the patient who in their household or friendship group could walk with them regularly, helping them identify a support network that already exists rather than referring them to a paid service). Prevention and control also accepted with equivalent development.

practice_questions.text:
Sanjay is 52 years old and works in a call centre. He was recently told his blood pressure is borderline high and his BMI is 28.1. His GP wants to support him to make lifestyle changes rather than immediately prescribing medication.

Discuss how the GP could use health promotion strategies to support Sanjay to take responsibility for his own health.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Addresses at least two health promotion strategies with developed reasoning, both linked to Sanjay's specific circumstances (borderline hypertension, overweight BMI, sedentary call-centre job). Education (Sanjay needs information about the link between his lifestyle and his readings, in a format he can act on — because without understanding the connection, he is unlikely to change); strengths-based (asking Sanjay what he enjoys and what small changes he feels able to make builds on his agency rather than imposing a plan); prevention and control (teaching Sanjay to monitor his own blood pressure at home gives him a tool to track his own progress). Considers challenges: Sanjay's sedentary work and possibly limited time for exercise. Uses 'because' and 'therefore'.

Secure (3–4 marks): Addresses at least one strategy with development and some reference to Sanjay.

Developing (2 marks): Names a strategy but limited development; limited link to Sanjay.

Emerging (1 mark): Names a strategy with no development.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the extent to which raising awareness through national health campaigns is an effective strategy for promoting health and well-being across the population.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (9–10 marks): Balanced evaluation of national campaigns as a health promotion strategy. Strengths: reach — a well-resourced national campaign (e.g. NHS Better Health) can reach millions of people through television, social media and GP signposting, a scale no individual practitioner can match; they raise awareness across the population, meaning even people who do not access health services may be reached; they normalise health-seeking behaviour and positive lifestyle choices. Limitations: awareness does not guarantee behaviour change — knowing that exercise is good does not mean people exercise more; campaigns may not reach the most deprived communities who face structural barriers to health (cost, access, time, housing); they may be more effective for already-motivated individuals and less so for those who need more personalised support. Comparison: campaigns are more effective when combined with local delivery, individual education and strengths-based approaches — the evidence shows that population-level messaging plus individual support is more effective than either alone. Conclusion: national campaigns are a valuable and necessary component of health promotion but are insufficient on their own; their effectiveness is maximised when they are integrated with local and individual-level support.

Secure (6–8 marks): Addresses most strengths and limitations with some development and a conclusion.

Developing (3–5 marks): Notes some strengths and limitations; limited conclusion.

Emerging (1–2 marks): One-sided or very brief response.

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the four purposes of health promotion?
options: Reduce health and social care costs

knowledge_checks.q: What does a strengths-based approach to health promotion focus on?
options: Identifying and documenting the individual's medical conditions
Building on the individual's existing strengths, capabilities and informal networks
Prescribing the most effective medication for the individual's condition
Referring the individual to specialist hospital services

knowledge_checks.q: Health promotion supports individuals to take _____ for their own health, rather than making them dependent on services.
Educating individuals by providing _____ and advice enables them to make positive lifestyle choices.
Match each health promotion purpose to its description:
right: Help individuals understand health issues they may not know about
Encourage vaccination, safer practices and reduced harmful behaviours
Prevention is cheaper than long-term treatment of preventable conditions

flashcard_questions.q: Name the four purposes of health promotion.
flashcard_questions.a: Raise awareness, increase positive lifestyle choices, reduce health risks, and reduce health and social care costs.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does reducing health and social care costs matter as a purpose of health promotion?
flashcard_questions.a: Prevention is cheaper than treating preventable chronic conditions long-term.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a strengths-based approach to health promotion?
flashcard_questions.a: Building on an individual's existing strengths and informal networks rather than focusing on deficits.

flashcard_questions.q: Name three strategies for supporting individuals to take responsibility for their own health.
flashcard_questions.a: Prevention and control; education through information and advice; encouraging personal strengths and informal networks.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between local and national health promotion?
flashcard_questions.a: National campaigns reach large populations via mass media; local delivery reaches individuals through trusted community contacts.

flashcard_questions.q: What are 'health campaigns' in a health promotion context?
flashcard_questions.a: Planned public health activities designed to change awareness, attitudes or behaviours at population scale.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is raising awareness alone usually insufficient for behaviour change?
flashcard_questions.a: Knowing about health risks does not guarantee that individuals will change their behaviour.

flashcard_questions.q: What does 'prevention and control' mean as a health promotion strategy?
flashcard_questions.a: Providing individuals with information and tools to prevent health problems or manage existing conditions.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one example of health promotion through informal networks.
flashcard_questions.a: Encouraging a service user to involve a family member or friend in their exercise routine for peer support.

flashcard_questions.q: How does health promotion link to active participation and person-centred care?
flashcard_questions.a: Effective health promotion involves individuals as active participants in their own health decisions, not passive recipients of advice.

glossary_terms.definition: Any activity or strategy designed to improve the health and well-being of individuals and communities, by raising awareness, enabling positive lifestyle choices, and supporting people to take responsibility for their own health.
Planned, coordinated public health activities designed to change awareness, attitudes or behaviours across a population in relation to a health issue.
An approach to supporting individuals that identifies and builds on their existing strengths, capabilities and resources rather than focusing primarily on deficits and needs.

items.title: How to Motivate Yourself to Change Behaviour | Tali Sharot | TEDxCambridge
items.description: Neuroscientist Sharot's evidence on what actually motivates health behaviour change — directly relevant to why information alone is insufficient for health promotion.

items.title: Why Good Leaders Make You Feel Safe | Simon Sinek | TED
items.description: Sinek explores trust and safety in organisations — the same strengths-based principles that underpin effective health promotion in care settings.

items.title: Why Comfort Will Ruin Your Life | Bill Eckstrom | TEDx
items.description: Examines how growth happens at the edge of comfort — supports the health promotion argument that individuals need challenge and support, not just information, to change.

items.title: Super Size Me 2: Holy Chicken! (2017)
items.description: Morgan Spurlock revisits the fast-food industry — useful for discussing how health promotion competes with commercial food marketing and why lifestyle change is complex.

items.title: NHS Better Health — Healthy Living Hub
items.description: The central NHS health promotion platform — covers healthy eating, activity, quitting smoking and more. Students can see what national health promotion looks like in practice.

items.title: Office for Health Improvement and Disparities (OHID) — Public Health Tools
items.description: The UK government's public health evidence hub — includes local health profiles and PHE campaign archives used by health promoters at local and national levels.

items.title: NICE — Health Promotion and Well-being Guidance
items.description: The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence publishes evidence-based guidance used by practitioners — demonstrates how health promotion recommendations are made.

items.title: The King's Fund — What Makes Us Healthy?
items.description: The King's Fund's accessible briefing on the wider determinants of health — explains why individual-level health promotion must be paired with structural change.
